title: Agentic AI Implementation Path: Course Completion Exam
description: Timed practice exam covering the whole series. Pass with 72% or higher to earn the course completion certificate.

questions.question: What distinguishes ReAct from a plain tool-calling loop?
options: It skips tool calls entirely and answers straight from the model's memory.
It interleaves reasoning with each action and observation.
It plans the entire task once before acting.
It runs several agents in parallel.
questions.explanation: ReAct interleaves a natural-language reasoning trace with each action and observation, so the model reasons before it acts instead of firing tools blindly.

questions.question: What does an open circuit breaker change about a request to a provider that is down?
options: The request is rejected fast instead of waiting on a timeout
The request is buffered until the provider recovers
The request is retried more aggressively until it finally succeeds
The request is routed to a faster model automatically
questions.explanation: When the breaker is open, requests fail immediately or skip to the fallback instead of each burning a full timeout. That fast rejection is what separates a clean failover from a cascading slowdown.

questions.question: A vector database backup can meet the database recovery point and still fail the retrieval recovery point. Why?
options: The physical backup was taken just before the final write had actually been committed to disk, so the last record was lost
The restore finished faster than the recovery time objective that the team had previously allowed for
Rows restore cleanly, but search returns stale chunks or mixed embedding versions, so retrieval was not restored
The backup captured the vectors but forgot to capture the operating system state as well
questions.explanation: Database recovery restores rows, but retrieval correctness also depends on the index and embedding model version, so a clean restore can still leave search stale or semantically mixed.

questions.question: An orchestrator-worker design with parallel subagents outperforms one agent searching in a single window because:
options: Independent context windows let subagents cover different branches in parallel
One very large context window is always cheaper and more reliable than several small ones
Subagents should share a single context window so each can see all the others' findings
A single agent can hold the entire search log and still finish reliably within budget
questions.explanation: Parallel subagents win where a question has many independent branches, because each can work a branch in its own context window instead of one window overflowing.

questions.question: In an agent loop, what is the reliable way to confirm the goal has actually been met?
options: Trust the model's own confident assessment that it is done
Count how many iterations the loop has run
Add a deterministic gate that verifies the result
Check that the context window is not yet full
questions.explanation: The model's judgment that it is finished can be confidently wrong, so a deterministic external gate must verify the result before the loop declares success.

questions.question: Why must an approval gate live in the runtime rather than in the system prompt?
options: Model providers reject any prompt that names more than one tool
A prompt is guidance a model may ignore; a runtime gate always fires
System prompts cannot persist across the steps of a tool-calling loop
A runtime cannot read a tool definition that the model was given
questions.explanation: A control must be a mechanism the runtime enforces, not a preference the model may or may not follow; a prompt only asks, while a deterministic gate holds.

questions.question: An agent answers smoothly but keeps formatting its output in prose when a strict structure is required. What kind of gap is this, and which approach fits?
options: A knowledge gap, because the model lacks the specific documents that describe the required output structure
A behavior gap, because the model knows the material but gets the form wrong, which fine-tuning fits
A retrieval gap, because a larger and better-indexed vector store would impose the correct format on the output
A cost gap, because only a smaller and cheaper model can be made to follow the required output structure
questions.explanation: The model knows the content but produces the wrong form, which is a behavior gap: format and style are durable behaviors that fine-tuning is suited to carry in the weights.

questions.question: Within a serverless platform, what is the main design consequence of the hard cap on how long one invocation may run?
options: It changes nothing, because a warmed execution environment can be reused across an effectively unlimited run of separate invocations that keep reusing the same warm container
It forces fast request-response work to fit inside the cap while durable batch work is consumed one unit per invocation behind a queue
It means a single invocation must run an agent's entire loop to completion before it may return any answer to the caller
It applies only to edge runtimes and never to container-based services such as a request-driven container platform
questions.explanation: Because each invocation has a fixed time budget, a long agent task cannot run in one call: fast answers return within the cap, while the batch backlog is drained one unit of work per invocation behind a queue.

questions.question: What distinguishes an integration test of an agent from a unit test?
options: It scores real model output with an LLM judge against a golden set
It runs the whole loop against controlled tool side effects
It measures the cost per request under sustained production load
It stubs the model and asserts only on a prompt string
questions.explanation: An integration test runs the real loop with mocked tools that return fixed data, so it can assert on tool selection, arguments, ordering, and that nothing destructive ran.

questions.question: How should a canary release of a new prompt behave for a conversational agent?
options: Compare the canary against a historical monthly baseline and redeploy to roll back
Route each request independently so traffic mixes freely between both versions
Split a small slice of traffic and compare the two versions against each other
Wait for full rollout before scoring any quality metric from the canary
questions.explanation: The canary and the stable version run concurrently and are compared with each other, rollback is an instant routing change rather than a redeploy, and conversational agents are pinned by session.

questions.question: An engineer presents a live demo of an agent succeeding on several cases and offers it as proof the design is sound. Why does a reviewer discount that?
options: Because demos are not allowed in a design review, since only the packet may be presented
Because a demo proves a path exists once, not that it is the normal path
Because the sample was too small to compute a rate, so the whole run must be repeated
Because the output cannot be reproduced, which makes the demo inadmissible as evidence
questions.explanation: A demo shows that a path exists on one day; under stochastic behavior it does not show that the path is the normal path. The evidence page therefore carries a pass rate, a sample size and one honest failing case.

questions.question: An agent struggles on a JavaScript-heavy page where the page structure is noisy but the screen is clear. Which approach fits best?
options: Use only the accessibility tree, since it always reflects everything on the page.
Use only full screenshots, since the structured signal can never help on any page.
Use the structured signal, falling back to screenshots when it runs out.
Disable the step cap so the agent can keep retrying the same click forever.
questions.explanation: The hybrid approach defaults to the cheap structured signal, such as the accessibility tree or DOM, and falls back to screenshots on visual or noisy pages. Routing per task beats committing to a single way of seeing.

questions.question: A model keeps producing worse output as more instructions are added to the prompt. What does this reflect?
options: Each added token depletes a finite attention budget and degrades recall
The model runs out of storage space for new instructions once the prompt grows long
The prompt text is being translated into another language
The system has exceeded its provider rate limit
questions.explanation: Recall falls as the context fills, so redundant context spends attention that the model needs for the actual task.

questions.question: A support agent needs a consistent brand voice and a strict summary format, plus answers grounded in a policy that changes monthly. What does the framework suggest?
options: Fine-tune only, because baking the policy into the weights is the cheapest way to keep the voice consistent
Retrieve only, because a retrieval layer can also teach the model a consistent voice and output format
A hybrid: fine-tune the durable behavior while retrieval supplies the current facts at answer time
Neither, because you cannot combine a tuned model with a retrieval step in one system
questions.explanation: Voice and format are stable behaviors that fine-tuning can hold, while a policy that changes monthly is current knowledge that retrieval should supply, so the mature answer is the hybrid.

questions.question: What does it mean to treat a tool schema as an operational contract?
options: It defines the inputs, outputs, and error path
It locks the tool to a single model provider
It documents the tool only for human developers
It removes the need to validate arguments at runtime
questions.explanation: The schema is the agreement among the model, your application, and the backend, and its error path is part of that agreement rather than an afterthought.

questions.question: Before any ranking, what does a metadata filter on retrieved chunks decide?
options: Which chunks are eligible to be returned
How many chunks the model is allowed to see
The order the chunks are passed to the model
How similar each chunk is to the query
questions.explanation: Metadata filtering sets eligibility, scope, and access before ranking, so the model never sees a chunk the user cannot see.

questions.question: Why should a platform's control plane be portable and attached to the asset rather than to one cloud's native tooling?
options: Because native cloud governance is always slower than a custom control plane.
Because no cloud vendor offers any governance tooling for agents at all.
Because asset-aware governance is required by law in every jurisdiction.
Because governance written in one cloud's schema cannot move to another.
questions.explanation: Governance expressed in a vendor's proprietary constructs is non-transferable: a multi-cloud portfolio needs separate stacks in separate policy languages, and the tooling that looked free at signup becomes the lock-in at exit. Governing by what the asset is keeps policy portable.

questions.question: Why is a customer ID on its own still treated as personal data in an agent pipeline?
options: Because any identifier that can point to a person counts as personal data
Because customer IDs always contain a name embedded somewhere in the string
Because only data that names a person explicitly is considered regulated
Because IDs are treated as personal data only once they are stored
questions.explanation: Personal data covers anything that can identify a person directly or in combination with other information, so recognition must span the assembled context rather than only obvious fields like a name.

questions.question: An agent must reproduce every cell of a dense table exactly for downstream processing. Which approach fits the task?
options: A general vision model reading the page at high detail in a single pass.
A text-only model given a short summary of the table's contents.
A specialized extraction pipeline tuned for exact table structure.
A general model asked to describe the table's overall meaning in prose.
questions.explanation: Flexible in-context reasoning suits a general multimodal model, but exact, high-volume reproduction of tables and charts is where a specialized extractor wins on accuracy and speed. The choice is a routing decision per task, not one tool for everything.

questions.question: An agent workflow stays net positive across a wide range of auto-clear rates. What carries that result?
options: A low enough token price that the inference line stops mattering
A high reversal cost that protects the workflow from being undone
A larger build budget that spreads platform cost over many runs
Packet preparation that shortens each remaining human decision
questions.explanation: The value comes less from autonomy than from packet preparation that makes every remaining human decision faster. The agent does not have to be right to be useful; it has to shorten the next decision.

questions.question: Why is cosine similarity the standard way to compare two embeddings?
options: It compares the direction of the vectors, not their length
It returns the exact number of shared words between the inputs
It normalizes both vectors to the same number of dimensions
It measures the raw distance between the two points in space
questions.explanation: Cosine similarity compares the angle between the vectors, so it captures direction of meaning rather than magnitude.

questions.question: What is the defining test of a real kill switch?
options: It asks the model to stop once it detects that it is looping
It pauses a single action until a person approves or rejects it
It can stop every running instance without the agent's cooperation
It records the runaway so a person can stop it after reviewing the record
questions.explanation: A kill switch is deterministic and external: it must be able to end the run without the agent's consent, which is why it is a cap the system enforces rather than a tool the agent chooses to call.

questions.question: Why is browser automation more exposed to prompt injection than a tool call you wrote yourself?
options: Browsers automatically strip all embedded text out of a page before a model can read it.
The page content the agent must read can itself carry hidden instructions.
Injected instructions can only ever change a chat answer and never a real action.
Web pages are always authored by the same user who asked the agent to visit them.
questions.explanation: A tool call has a defined shape you control, but a browsing agent must read the web, and the content it reads is the same channel an attacker can use to give it orders. That is why its guardrails assume content is untrusted rather than relying on the model to ignore attacks.

questions.question: Before rolling back or restarting an agent after confirming an incident, what must happen first?
options: Delete the affected session logs so that the bad behavior is not preserved in long-term storage
Revert to the last known-good prompt so the agent stops taking harmful actions
Export or snapshot the incident window's trace to storage independent of production
Restart the agent to clear its in-memory state before the investigation begins
questions.explanation: Recovery destroys evidence: a rollback swaps the running version and a restart clears in-memory state. The trace must be frozen to independent storage before any recovery action, or the record of what happened is lost.

questions.question: The while loop that repeatedly calls the model and executes tools is best understood as whose responsibility?
options: Runtime or framework code, not something you write
A portion you must hand-code yourself for every agent you build
A detail that varies by which model you choose
The same thing as the system prompt you author
questions.explanation: The loop itself is runtime code; your work lives in what the loop touches, such as tools and schemas, state, stopping criteria, logging, and memory.

questions.question: What gives a coding agent a verifier it can run on its own?
options: Code either compiles or passes tests or it does not, and the agent can run that check itself
A human must review and approve every single edit the agent proposes before it is allowed to continue
The agent guesses whether its change looks correct and then proceeds to the next step anyway
An external service grades the agent's output after each session has fully finished and ended
questions.explanation: A coding agent's success signal is a check that runs itself, such as a test suite or build, so verification is the closing phase of each loop rather than an external human step.

questions.question: Why treat prompts with the same version-tracking as code?
options: Because it shortens the file name and makes each prompt easier to type into a terminal during a deployment
Because two prompts can be a comma apart yet behave completely differently, so history and rollback matter
Because it is the only format an open-source evaluation tool will accept when it runs the test cases
Because it forces a full application redeploy on every wording change, which is the intended safety net
questions.explanation: Prompts are production behavior: two nearly identical prompts can behave very differently, so a real version history, a rollback path, and a record of which version runs where are all needed.

questions.question: What single property best distinguishes an agent from a workflow?
options: The model, not your code, decides the path
The system includes at least one call to a language model
The system can handle more than one request per session
The system was assembled with a modern agent framework
questions.explanation: An agent is defined by who decides the path: the model directs its own process and tool use at runtime, while in a workflow your code fixes the path and the model only fills the steps.

questions.question: A team reports that every analyst finished the required training session and asks to go live. What does a working readiness gate require in addition?
options: A completion dashboard with per-person timestamps so the sponsor can see training landed
A scored dry run on real cases with a stated threshold and a dated retry
A second refresher session scheduled thirty days after launch to review the material
A signed attendance sheet recording which analysts were present at every session
questions.explanation: Finishing a session shows that information was received, not that it can be applied under real conditions. A working gate uses real cases, scores the decisions against a stated threshold, and gives anyone who fails a dated retry.

questions.question: Which latency number matters most for a human who reads an answer as it arrives?
options: End-to-end latency, because it measures the whole response
Time to first token, because the reader stops waiting
Time per output token, because faster tokens read better
Batch size, because it sets how responsive the reply feels
questions.explanation: Once the stream outpaces reading speed, the only wait a person consciously feels is the silence before the first token. For a human reader, time to first token is the experience.

questions.question: Why should raw source records be normalized before they reach the embedding model?
options: Raw payloads waste embedding budget on structural noise and dilute attention, producing low-quality vectors
Normalization allows the embedding model to choose all of its own chunk boundaries directly from the raw source text
Normalization removes the need to chunk the text because the model handles whole documents
The embedding model can reliably separate the semantic signal from syntax without any help
questions.explanation: The embedding model cannot tell meaning from syntax, so structural noise consumes the token budget and pulls attention away from the text that carries the semantic signal.

questions.question: An agent stores every message forever and surfaces a fact that was true last month but is not anymore. What is the flaw?
options: It never consolidates or demotes outdated facts
It sends too little context to the model each turn
It keeps the context window smaller than the store
It mixes episodic and semantic memory in one table
questions.explanation: An unbounded store that is never consolidated keeps stale facts at the same standing as current ones, so the agent confidently repeats what is no longer true.

questions.question: What distinguishes an agentic workflow from an autonomous pipeline?
options: The workflow can act without approval, while the pipeline always requires a person to start each run
The workflow fixes the sequence, while the pipeline moves work unattended and survives a crash
The workflow runs on a schedule, while the pipeline is triggered by a person each time
The workflow tolerates crashes, while the pipeline is expected to restart from the beginning
questions.explanation: An agentic workflow runs model and tool calls through a fixed code path, so the sequence is set at design time. An autonomous pipeline moves work between systems unattended, and its own failure is lost or duplicated work rather than a wrong answer.

questions.question: Why is a managed platform generally the hardest path to leave?
options: Because the vendor publishes its orchestration code openly for anyone to reuse.
Because nothing you build on it ever touches your own data or systems.
Because you never own the state, routing, or code that runs your loop.
Because managed platforms can never ship a working demo quickly.
questions.explanation: Leaving a managed platform means reimplementing orchestration you never wrote and porting state you never saw, so the convenience that sped up onboarding is paid back on exit. The general rule is that the faster something lets you ship, the more it costs to leave.

questions.question: How does a multimodal model connect a word in a prompt to the region of an image it refers to?
options: Cross-attention in a shared embedding space that binds words to image regions.
A separate OCR pass that turns the image into text before the language model runs.
A captioning step that replaces the image with a written description of it first.
The language model is discarded so only the vision encoder produces the answer.
questions.explanation: Each modality is encoded, projected into one shared embedding space, then fused by cross-attention, which lets one modality selectively attend to parts of another. That is what binds a word to the pixels it names.

questions.question: Which failure should not be retried because retrying it only delays a fix?
options: A rate-limited response that will clear
A temporary service-unavailable response
An unauthorized response from bad credentials
A gateway timeout from an overloaded upstream
questions.explanation: An unauthorized response is a permanent failure on your side, like a malformed request or a wrong endpoint. Retrying it wastes time and hides the real configuration bug; only transient server-side failures are worth retrying.

questions.question: In the MCP architecture, what is the client?
options: A separate machine that runs both the model and the whole orchestration
A component inside the host, created once per server connection
The remote program that exposes tools, prompts, and data
The end user's browser session that opens the connection
questions.explanation: The client is not a separate machine: it lives inside the host and the host creates one client object for each server it connects to, handling that single connection's protocol messages.

questions.question: In the canonical agent loop, what signal tells the code that the agent is done?
options: A response that contains only plain text and no tool calls.
A response that contains at least one tool call for the code to run.
A response that exceeds the token budget for the run.
A response that repeats a previous tool call it already made.
questions.explanation: A text-only response is the termination signal; a response with tool calls is the continuation signal that keeps the loop running.

questions.question: Why does a good evaluation set include cases drawn from real production traffic rather than only clean synthetic examples?
options: Synthetic examples are always too long to use inside a gate.
Real traffic carries the edge cases that clean examples miss.
Production data never contains any personal or sensitive information at all.
A judge can only score inputs that it has already seen before.
questions.explanation: Datasets built only from documentation or synthetic generation come out too clean and miss the edge cases and adversarial inputs real users produce.

questions.question: When you gate which actions an agent may take, why is an allowlist safer than a denylist?
options: An allowlist denies by default, so anything you did not think to list is refused.
An allowlist runs its checks faster than a denylist can at runtime.
A denylist cannot express a rule that blocks more than one value at a time.
A denylist requires the model itself to confirm every blocked action before it runs.
questions.explanation: An allowlist denies by default and fails closed on anything unnamed, while a denylist admits by default and lets through whatever you forgot to list.

questions.question: Why do shared standards cut integration cost?
options: Because custom links grow with pairs of systems, while a shared standard needs one implementation each
Because a standard removes the commercial questions of liability, data use and uptime from the relationship
Because a published protocol makes two compliant implementations agree on what a message means
Because a standard lets any system connect without authentication once both sides share the protocol
questions.explanation: Adapters are counted per pair, so cost grows with pairs of systems rather than with systems. One shared standard needs a single implementation per system and cuts the pairwise count sharply.

questions.question: How should the tool boundary be drawn for a support agent?
options: Give the agent both read and write tools to keep the whole design simple
Keep write tools in the prompt so the model gates its own actions
Let the agent hold the billing credentials so it can act directly
Default every tool to read-only and add write tools under guard
questions.explanation: Starting read-only caps the blast radius: a tool that returns order status is safe to deploy broadly, while a tool that writes or refunds is added only behind its own policy check.

questions.question: Why is cost per completed task a better metric to manage than cost per token?
options: Per-token prices fall while total bills rise, because work per task grows faster and hidden retries stay invisible
Per-token pricing is never published by providers at all, so the figure cannot be reconciled against a monthly invoice or used in a forecast
Per-token cost counts only generated output and ignores every input token the agent sends
Per-token cost is always the higher figure, so finance has more room to negotiate a lower contract
questions.explanation: A task bill grows even as unit prices fall, because the work one task performs multiplies across planning, tool calls, retries, and sub-agents. Cost per completed task captures that real spend, while cost per token hides it.

questions.question: An agent loads a peer's published capability card and its skill examples into its own context. What stance is correct?
options: The card is authoritative, so a declared capability is enough authorization to delegate
A valid signature proves the peer is trustworthy, so its returned outputs need no further validation on your side at all
The card can be ignored at runtime because the version changes too often to check
The card is a claim from a stranger: verify capabilities at runtime and treat its text as untrusted data
questions.explanation: A card is an advertisement written by the party asking for work, and its free-form text becomes part of a prompt. A signature only proves origin, so delegation should follow your own policy and the card text should be treated as untrusted.

questions.question: The error budget burns most of its monthly allowance in two days after a bad change. What is the correct response?
options: Stop shipping changes until the budget recovers, rather than ship faster to fix things
Spend the remaining budget on the fix, since a budget exists to fund corrective changes
Roll the rollout back a stage and then resume shipping at the same rate
Raise the objective so the burn no longer breaches the documented threshold
questions.explanation: An objective is a budget to spend, and when it burns down the response is to stop shipping changes rather than to ship faster. Raising an objective to escape a burn defeats the purpose of having one.

questions.question: A tool the agent can call hits a bad input. Why return a readable error string instead of raising?
options: Raising hides the failure from the monitoring layer
Raising makes the tool slower to call on the next turn of the run
Raising ends the run, while a readable string lets it recover
Raising lets the tool skip its own input validation
questions.explanation: An enterprise tool that raises crashes the whole run, so it returns an error message the model can read and act on instead.

questions.question: Why is context treated as the scarce resource in a coding session?
options: Context space is effectively unlimited and cheap to fill, so filling the window faster always improves the agent's accuracy on any task
Every file read and command output fills the window, and quality degrades as it fills, so key information must stay accessible
Context only ever holds the final answer, so it rarely needs to be managed while a task runs
The window resets automatically after every tool call, so it almost never needs any attention
questions.explanation: A session accumulates file reads and command outputs, and model quality falls as the window fills, so keeping the important instructions in view is a design concern.

questions.question: What design feature lets a graph runtime support retries, pause-and-resume, and time-travel debugging?
options: A prompt that tells the model to remember its state.
A larger context window on the underlying model.
A shared, typed, checkpointable state object.
A team of role-based agents with backstories.
questions.explanation: The runtime persists a shared, typed state through checkpointing, which is what enables retries, pause-and-resume, and time-travel debugging.

questions.question: Before trusting an automated judge to gate releases, what should you do first?
options: Run it against human-reviewed labels and measure how often it agrees.
Raise its temperature so that the scores vary a good deal more.
Ask the judge to evaluate its own previous scores for consistency.
Replace it with the exact-match metrics that it was originally meant to replace.
questions.explanation: A judge is a probabilistic instrument, so you validate it against human-reviewed labels and measure agreement before letting it gate anything.

questions.question: What is the risk of a semantic cache with a loose similarity threshold?
options: It can return an answer that only resembles the question, which is a correctness bug
It stores every cached answer twice, roughly doubling the storage cost of the cache itself
It refuses almost every cache hit, calling the model for each request again
It slows the first call in each window while the cached prefix is written
questions.explanation: A semantic cache decides a hit by embedding similarity, so a loose threshold starts serving answers that merely resemble the question, which makes the threshold a correctness decision and not only a cost one.

questions.question: What does change data capture let a retrieval pipeline do?
options: Re-embed the entire corpus on every single run so that the index is always perfectly consistent and current
Replace the embedding model entirely with a fixed set of deterministic rules and mappings
See an event for each insert, update, and delete, so it can re-embed only the content that changed
Avoid needing a vector store at all by serving results directly from the source system
questions.explanation: Capturing change as a stream of insert, update, and delete events tells the pipeline exactly what moved, which is what makes it possible to re-embed only those records.

questions.question: In what order should the cost levers be applied, and why?
options: Cap, then cache, then route, since a budget ceiling stops overspending right away
Cache, then route across tiers, then cap and watch, since the first two set the amount spent
Watch first, then cap, then route, since a spend dashboard shows exactly where the money went
Route first, then watch, then cache, since per-token pricing gaps are the single biggest lever
questions.explanation: Caching and routing reduce how much is spent before any cap matters; a dashboard only reports where the money went, so reaching for it first leaves the bill unchanged.

questions.question: Which three question shapes does a knowledge graph genuinely beat plain vector memory on?
options: Text-similarity lookups, full-text keyword searches, and linguistic paraphrase recall across a document set
Standalone fact lookups, single-document summaries, and token-length optimization targets
Relationship-path multi-hop queries, whole-corpus aggregations, and dense interconnected domains
Image retrieval, numeric range filters, and fuzzy date matching across log files
questions.explanation: A graph wins where resemblance fails: relationship-path multi-hop questions, whole-corpus aggregations, and dense interconnected domains where everything looks similar to everything else.

questions.question: Why are documents split into chunks before they are embedded?
options: So the model can generate longer answers from each one
So each chunk fits the model limit and stands alone
So the same text never appears in more than one chunk
So chunk order is preserved when the index is rebuilt
questions.explanation: Embedding models have limited input length and a chunk must carry enough meaning to be found, so documents are split into self-contained pieces.

questions.question: Why can a web application firewall not serve as a complete semantic safety layer for an AI application?
options: It inspects only the response body and never the incoming request at all
It cannot be deployed in front of a model endpoint
It matches text patterns, not meaning, so rephrased attacks slip past it
It already enforces the authentication the gateway provides
questions.explanation: A firewall reads surface text, not meaning, so paraphrased or encoded injections evade its rules. Catching those requires a separate control that interprets the prompt.

questions.question: Why does cost per accepted output make a stronger denominator than cost per token or cost per seat?
options: It measures only the model spend, so it isolates the cost that scales with volume
It divides total cost by the work that a human accepts without redoing
It removes the need to estimate rework, since failures are not counted as outputs
It tracks how cheaply the model generates text, which is the figure finance reviews
questions.explanation: Cost per token is the bill and cost per seat is a software habit; neither says whether the spend was worthwhile. Dividing total cost by accepted outputs, including the rework failures require, is what makes the unit economics computable.

questions.question: What is the role of a system prompt in an agent?
options: A one-time instruction sent only on the very first turn
The persistent instruction block used on every turn
A fallback used only when the model fails
An optional courtesy message shown to the user
questions.explanation: Because the loop re-sends it on each turn, the system prompt acts as the agent's constitution: the durable role, rules, and output format it obeys throughout.

questions.question: A local model accepts OpenAI-style tool calls but returns JSON that fails to parse. What does this demonstrate?
options: The model needs a larger context window to emit valid JSON
Compatible wire format does not guarantee reliable calls
Local models cannot support tool calling in any configuration
The schema must be rewritten in the provider's native dialect
questions.explanation: A provider can speak a compatible wire format yet still return malformed or incomplete arguments, so parsed arguments must be validated before a tool runs.

questions.question: What is the difference between a routing destination and a router?
options: A destination runs a request; the router picks which one
A destination decides routing; the router only measures latency
A destination is a local model; a router is a managed service
A destination and a router are two names for the same thing
questions.explanation: A destination is a place a request runs, while the router is the decision layer that chooses among destinations, so calling one provider directly is an integration, not routing.

questions.question: What is the recommended approach to reaching for a multi-agent design?
options: Always use several agents for any real task.
Prefer it whenever more than one model is available.
Start simple and add coordination only when a single agent pays a real cost.
Use a coordinator whenever a task can be broken into any number of separate steps.
questions.explanation: Start with the simplest single agent and add coordination only when you can point to a real cost it is paying, since every extra agent adds nondeterminism and cost.
